items.content: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) My new book is out today... what happened since the last one Ethan Mollick Oct 20, 2026 792 142 67 Share My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.” Some examples of interacting with Claude to make the graphics for this post. Notice that it corrected me. “This is the worst AI you will ever use” I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence , and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI. Which company had the best AI model in the world. But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone. items.content: The Dot and the Swarm - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Dot and the Swarm Benefitting from the Bitter Lesson Ethan Mollick Oct 01, 2026 1,393 235 142 Share I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with agents as a manager, deciding how to delegate work to agents and specifying how those agents should be organized. I thought that getting agents to work effectively as a group would take careful construction, akin to building a company, and that this would take time to figure out. Nope. I fell prey to The Bitter Lesson, the hard truth, learned over and over again, that things that we thought required elaborate human rules and thinking can be solved with the brute force of better machine learning systems and more AI. The Bitter Lesson is everywhere among AI startups and companies adopting AI. A huge amount of effort went into building elaborate computer systems to feed AIs the right information at the right time, but AI systems have learned to seek out information themselves. The same thing happened to prompting. People built elaborate templates and chains of prompts that walked the AI through a task one step at a time. Then newer models turned out to be better at planning the steps themselves, and, as our research shows , planning steps have much less value. The history of the Bitter Le— — you know what? I don’t really need to explain the Bitter Lesson, I asked Claude to do it in a music video. With one prompt, Fable wrote the lyrics and submitted it to Suno; Opus 5.5 did everything else using code alone without any image generation (How did Opus 5.5 pull this off? The Bitter Lesson tells you!). I gave no feedback at all. As somebody who teaches managers and has published research on management, I guess I believed that managing agents would be different. items.content: The Overhang - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Overhang Using your deep knowledge, wide knowledge, taste, and agency Ethan Mollick Sep 18, 2026 960 119 105 Share We are still on an exponential curve of AI development. I try to put out a Substack post every couple weeks or so, yet, as the pace speeds up, that sometimes feels too slow. In the weeks since my last post, we had the apparent cracking of one of the most famous problems in math by an AI (accompanied by controversy) and widespread discussions about the risks posed by AI and what to do about it (also accompanied by controversy). I think these concerns, along with a mounting set of other worries, come down to the same problem I have with my posts: how slowly our very human systems and processes work to keep up with the pace of AI development. I don't think the people worried about this are wrong, but I also think a sole focus on future AIs, as important as that is, ignores the fact that AI, right now, is already incredibly capable. In fact, the new GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 are already enough for transformative impact in large sections of the economy and they can reliably do weeks worth of human work when properly guided and harnessed. A few fun examples of that: I had GPT-6 Astra turn a 1977 text adventure game called Zork into a full 3D action-adventure game you can play . Zork has no graphics and each location is a paragraph of prose, so the AI had to decide what the white house looks like, what a grue looks like (the original only tells you that you are likely to be eaten by one in the dark), and how to turn “fight the troll” into an action sequence. I also had Fable 5.1 try to reconstruct Italian author Umberto Eco’s library in 3D . Eco kept tens of thousands of books in his Milan apartment and the AI could not find a floor plan, so it instead decided to work from a dozen videos, the foundation's photographs of each bookcase, and two library catalogues. It read spines frame by frame, inferred the rooms, and placed the 5,000 or so books it could identify among 27,000 shelf slots. It marked every book certain, guess, or unknown, and drew the bookcases the cameras never reached in fog. This task, like the Zork game and a lot of real-world work I have had the AI do recently, would have taken weeks of human work involving researchers, coders, and designers. But here we are. items.content: if you feel behind right now don’t worry you aren’t Subscribe Sign in Finding my thing Nobody knows anything Nov 03, 2026 42 8 1 Share How do I follow up my last post…I’ve never had such a response before, I’m still working my way through every reply. And I wasn’t actually going to post today. Since last week I’ve been having great conversations and spent a lot of time thinking, without my agent. I’m back to actually jotting stuff down in my notes rather than agents. Inertia is my problem. Just because this newsletter is sent tues/thurs in a specific format, it’s easier to keep that going. I feel obliged. But really I’m trying to find something. My thing . And if I do what I’ve done, I won’t find it. I need to change it up. So from now until the end of the year, the formats will vary, the content, even the days + frequency of when I post. I’m in experimental mode. The digital equivalent of going to Thailand, slinging on those awful trousers and finding myself. I need to post what I’m interested in. For me to continue doing this for a long time, I have to make these for me. So what am I interested in? I’m following my nose. It’s already led me to have convos with Stripe, Granola, Zed and Raycast about how they’re building in this new world, while staying sane and nurturing a considered culture. I think there’s a ton of interesting stuff here I’ll write and build on top of. Coming soon-ish. I said I wasn’t going to post today, but you’re reading this…so, what gives? Well in my deliberation of to post or not to post, I felt like I wanted to bring you along in my thinking. I want to bare all whilst we see where we end up. I’ve stopped using Grok Bot for everything, except to ping me when Carlos Alcaraz is playing. I’m reading more long-form. I’m consuming less slop (and spending a little less time on X). I’m recording a voice-note every morning for a minimum of 10 minutes, and not doing anything with the transcript. I’m letting things percolate, noticing what I come back to. Agents give you answers to everything. But if we’re ‘soul-searching’ or trying to connect the dots, an answer presented to us may not be the right path. Even if it’s a reasonable one. All I’m ‘optimising’ for here is - what do I really want to do? And noticing what I keep coming back to when I take the time to think on it. This is not an ‘anti-ai’ stance at all. I love AI. I can do so much more than I ever could. It’s a tool though, not a person, and I use it as such. You probably need a grand total of one tool (an agent). Instead of looking at everything as an opportunity to optimise, I want to use AI for fun. Quick bites Try doubleAI’s Maxwell , a code execution model that speeds up software as it runs. Results: 38x faster data pipelines with no code changes.* Patrick Collison posted about adding a feedback box to what you build as a quick way to keep iterating. A few links to get your agents to make good UI: Stageshow for making product demos, BoardUI for great-looking compone

items.content: AI is overwhelming and I’m doing it wrong - Ben's Bites Subscribe Sign in AI is overwhelming and I’m doing it wrong Let’s think about what we’re doing here Oct 29, 2026 74 16 11 Share Let’s talk about this… Ben Tossell @ bentossell i feel stuck with wtf i do for like 10 months keep going round in circles. questioning and re-questioning everything. things feel exciting then dont. what feels like a good business direction then doesnt. touch grass, ai melting brains, i know i know but still 8:41 AM · Oct 28, 2026 · 82.5K Views 163 Replies · 9 Reposts · 681 Likes Where do I even start? It seems like a lot of people are feeling this too. The constant barrage of new products, models, capabilities, threats, whatever is one thing. But seeing people with 20 personal agents for managing their social content or just life. What are we doing here?! When I first started the newsletter it was to keep up with everything that was going on. It was 5 days a week. It was so noisy I decided to cut it down (along with our revenue) to just two days. I try and cut through the noise with the links here but the noise is still there, it may be louder. I read two excellent posts yesterday. Here’s a snippet from each You’re doing your best to keep up. You’re 9-9-6’ing, sometimes 0-0-7’ing. You didn’t actually rest during rest week, did you? What are your agents up to? Hopefully getting a lot done while you’re reading this. Have you tried the latest personal assistant? Optimized your workflows to accommodate the strengths of the latest model? Have you gone viral on X lately? Have you been angel investing? Have you locked in your Bay Area mortgage? If not, you know you’re fucked, right? You’re enslaved to your keyboard, timeline, and Slack. You’re tired, but your ambition is also Icarus-ing. Your FOMO is spiking. Your capacity is redlining. Is your moral compass spinning? Oh, and you don’t even have to type it anymore. Hands too sore? items.content: How big is the open model economy today? Subscribe Sign in How big is the open model economy today? Our first open model economy research note for paid subscribers. Nathan Lambert Nov 04, 2026 ∙ Paid 44 3 Share My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access.
